teaser.text: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners (CCEP) is the company behind familiar drinks that reach shops, restaurants and cafés across Europe, Australia, the Pacific and Southeast Asia. It does not own every brand it sells: its business is to turn brand rights, ingredients, factories and delivery routes into drinks customers can buy, then keep what remains after its costs.

stock.opening: CCEP's weighted scenario is 7,989.06 GBp by October 2027, for a +1% return including dividends. It hinges on profit growth, cash conversion and a sustained premium valuation.
stock.closing: The full memo also answers what matters about CCEP’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could CCEP's shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The weighted value is 7,989.06 GBp by October 2027, a +1% return including dividends. Scenario probabilities are 27% bear, 53% base and 20% bull. The base case needs gradual margin expansion. The bear case reflects weak volume and cash conversion.

The weighted forecast expects almost no total return in October 2027, followed by modest gains. It rises to 7% in October 2028 and 14% by October 2029, including dividends. The final range is wide: 5071.15 GBp in the bear case to 13482.06 GBp in the bull case, against 8090.00 GBp today.

blocks.heading: What has to go right—and wrong—for CCEP?

paragraphs.text: The bear case holds earnings near €1,900m before slipping to €1,890m. Revenue moves from €22.0bn to €22.5bn and then €23.0bn, while margins narrow from 8.64% to 8.22%. Weak volume, affordability pressure and cost inflation drive the stall. The bull case reaches €2,300m, €2,520m and €2,760m as revenue rises from €23.0bn to €26.2bn and margins expand from 10.00% to 10.53%. H1 comparable revenue grew 6.1%, operating profit grew 8.1% and Zero Sugar grew 10.7%, but six extra consumption days make the evidence less conclusive.

The bull case requires Zero Sugar and energy growth to broaden, productivity to beat costs and Tarlac capacity to fill quickly. Stronger cash conversion must fund investment, buybacks and debt reduction together, sustaining a premium multiple. That produces 9920.73 GBp initially and 13482.06 GBp by the final date. The 20% probability reflects the need for several uncertain outcomes to succeed simultaneously.

blocks.heading: How much real free cash flow does CCEP make?

paragraphs.text: Profit is recorded when sales and expenses are recognised, while cash moves when customers and suppliers pay. Working capital captures that timing. In 2025 it absorbed €172 million, whereas it released €332 million in 2024. The earlier release helped cash, but cannot recur indefinitely.

dividend.title: CCEP dividend: pay, coverage and yield
dividend.meta_description: CCEP pays a rising dividend, but 2025 free cash flow did not cover total shareholder payments; see the yield, plans and risks.
dividend.opening: CCEP pays dividends, but in 2025 its free cash flow did not cover total shareholder payments. The cash shortfall came as CCEP also returned money through buybacks.
dividend.closing: The full memo also covers CCEP’s business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: How much does CCEP pay per share?

paragraphs.text: Base dividends rise to €2.25, €2.46 and €2.63 per share through a 50% payout. The bear case gives €1.80, €1.75 and €1.80 on a 40% payout, reflecting cash pressure. The bull case gives €2.42, €2.68 and €2.96 on a 52% payout. The base follows a dividend that rose every year from €1.40 in 2021 to €2.04 in 2025 and a stated 50% policy.

blocks.heading: Is CCEP’s dividend covered by its cash?

paragraphs.text: The 2025 change was the return of buybacks alongside dividends. CCEP generated €1,605 million of free cash flow but paid €1,969 million to shareholders. The €364 million gap came from the balance sheet, while net debt ended at €9,038 million and cash fell.

Free cash flow fell to €1,605 million. After stock-based compensation, which transfers value to employees through shares or future dilution, an economic calculation leaves €1,558 million. CCEP’s own measure was €1,836 million because it includes disposal proceeds and uses net interest paid. Selling property is cash, but it is not cash earned by selling another case of Coca-Cola.

paragraphs.text: For 2026, management guides to comparable, currency-neutral revenue growth of 3.0%–4.0% and operating-profit growth of 7.0%. It expects comparable free cash flow of at least €1,700 million, capital expenditure including leases of 5.0% of revenue, a 50.0% dividend payout ratio and €1,000 million of buybacks.
